Each task gives the agent a codebase that misbehaves and a description of the symptoms or the documentation it should follow.
The agent finds the faulty code, fixes it without breaking what already works, and in some tasks writes a report naming each root cause.
Hidden tests check both the fixes and the code that was already correct.
Gemini 4 Argon passes 25% of its runs on these tasks, and it fails every run on 71% of the tasks.
Gemini 3.8 Flash passes 7%, and it fails every run on 67% of the tasks.
The main languages are Python (60%) and Go (40%).

| Domain | What the tasks do | % of catalog |
|---|---|---:|
| Languages & developer tooling | Find and fix faults in command-line tools, a compiler, a logic-programming engine and a utility library.
Maintainers are handed code that is wrong in several places and must find the causes without a test suite to lean on.
In the diagnosis tasks, many undocumented edits break unrelated features at once.
In the documentation-drift tasks, the code still runs but contradicts its own documentation.
One task starts from a single production symptom with a hidden root cause.
In all of them the engineer reproduces the symptom, finds the faulty function and repairs it without breaking neighbouring behaviour.
Each task ships a pinned checkout of an open-source project, with the tests withheld and no network.
The prompt describes the symptoms or names the documentation in scope, never the location of the faults.
Most diagnosis tasks also ask for `/app/rca.json`, which lists the file and function of each edit and is compared with an answer key.
Drift tasks treat the documentation as the authority and forbid editing it.
Hidden tests check the repairs and the behaviour that was already correct.
A first-person list of symptoms grouped by feature, with no file or function named, ending in a request to fix and report.
A stated number of undocumented edits and a JSON schema for the root-cause report.
A library description with the source paths and documentation pages in scope, and the rule that documentation outranks code.

children.title: How it maps to the work

children.text: A maintainer of a Datalog engine receives a user report that undocumented single-line edits have broken parsing, type checking, evaluation, provenance and temporal arithmetic, and no test suite is available.
The maintainer starts from the faulted source tree and the written symptoms only.

The hard part is tracing each symptom to the function that holds the edit, including symptoms that need two separate fixes before they disappear, and then naming exactly those functions in a root-cause report.

children.title: How it maps to the work

children.text: A maintainer of a medical imaging library treats the documentation as the specification and repairs the places where the code has drifted from it.
The engineer starts from the source tree with its pages, docstrings and examples, and has no list of the discrepancies.

The hard part is reading a large documented surface of transforms, data containers and patch sampling closely enough to find each behavioral mismatch, fixing the code rather than the docs, and leaving every behavior that already matches untouched.

children.title: How it maps to the work

children.text: A machine learning engineer maintains an experiment tracker and receives a complaint that diverged sweep runs rank first in the exported CSV.

The engineer has to follow the NaN from the CSV plugin back to where the value is lost, repair it in the library so every consumer is fixed, add a regression test, and write down where the defect starts.
The work mirrors an incident ticket against a shared tool.
